title: Sourdough starter troubleshooting, hooch, off smells, and sluggish rise
subtitle: What the common problems look like and how to fix them
excerpt: A sourdough starter is a living culture and sometimes misbehaves. Hooch, a vinegary smell, an orange or pink discolouration, or a starter that refuses to rise are the most common problems. All of them are fixable. Most come down to temperature, feeding frequency, or flour quality.
sourceNotes: Sourdough starter troubleshooting is well-documented in practical home baking literature. The orange-pink streak problem caused by Serratia marcescens bacteria is a known contamination issue.

glossaryTerms.definition: A grey or brown liquid that forms on top of a neglected starter. It is alcohol produced by the yeast when there is no more starch to ferment. A sign the starter is hungry. Stir it back in or pour it off before feeding.

content.text: Most sourdough starter problems come from insufficient feeding, wrong temperature, or poor flour quality. Almost all of them are recoverable with a few days of consistent feeding.
Hooch (grey or brown liquid on top)
is alcohol, the yeast has eaten all available starch and switched to producing alcohol. Stir it back in for extra sour flavour, or pour it off for a milder starter. Feed immediately.

Over-acidification from infrequent feeding or a cold kitchen that has allowed the acid-producing bacteria to dominate. Feed twice a day with fresh flour and water for 2 to 3 days. Keep the starter at 21 to 24°C. The yeast should regain strength within 3 to 4 feeds.
Discard this starter and start again. Orange or pink colouration is caused by a bacterial contamination. A new starter from fresh flour and a clean jar is the only safe response.

Three possible causes: too cold (move to a warmer spot), too much chlorine in the tap water (use filtered water or leave tap water out overnight), or flour that has been treated with bleach or improvers that suppress yeast growth. Switch to wholemeal or rye flour for 3 to 4 feeds; both contain more wild yeast and will jump-start a sluggish culture.
Starter rises but bakes turn out flat

The culture is active but not strong enough yet for bread leavening. Continue daily feedings for 1 to 2 more weeks. Test regularly with the float test; bake when the starter doubles reliably within 4 to 8 hours and floats. A culture that is several weeks old and well-established produces noticeably more lift than one that is new.
